id: #104 from The Poems of Gaius Valerius Catullus

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

with Dana Ward with Dana Ward I have so little want of activity even writing with its pain more terrible than life I don’t want but do because I’m kind of stupid finally not in the way, you, Sarah know I am nor, you reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments for me are accessories, even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long & white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question” On the witness stand I am a kitten terribly cute but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lay at the base of a hill asleep while the shepherds work bringing things to heel with tepid will where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell which was sifted through the vale of tears, & fell to make Earth, & the base of this hill where I sunbathe & murmur ‘jealous cellmate’ as my willful peers go by.

### Option 1: Refined Literary Prose (Recommended)
> Alongside Dana Ward, I feel very little desire for activity. Even writing—with its agony more terrible than life itself—is something I do not wish to do, yet I undertake it out of a peculiar foolishness. It is not, ultimately, the kind of foolishness known to you, Sarah, nor to you, the reader, who picture me fishing. 
> 
> Line, spindle, lure, and bait: to me, such instruments are mere adornments. A matchbook appears to my eyes as a tiara, and a fishing lure as a long, white bracelet. Certain so-called friends regard me as a derelict, constantly attempting to hold me accountable, demanding: “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question.” Yet on the witness stand, I am like a disarmingly cute kitten, incapable of testifying about foolishness, fish, or the events of last night. 
> 
> I prefer to lie asleep at the foot of a hill while the shepherds toil, bringing creation to heel with their tepid willpower. It is there that I draw my contempt from the index of swill. The entries within make no mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears and fell to form the Earth—including the base of this hill where I sunbathe, murmuring “jealous cellmate” as my willful peers pass me by.

---

### Option 2: Elegant Stylized Verse/Prose 
> In the company of Dana Ward, I possess little appetite for action. Even the act of writing—bearing a pain more acute than life—is an unwanted burden I carry out of a subtle foolishness. It is not the foolishness you know me for, Sarah, nor that of you, reader, who envision me fishing. 
> 
> Line, spindle, lure, bait—these instruments are merely accessories to me. The matchbook is a tiara before my eyes; the fishing lure, a long, white bracelet. My so-called friends view me as a derelict, forever trying to hold me to account: *“Tell us what happened on the drunken night in question.”* On the witness stand, I am a terribly charming kitten, unable to utter a word regarding stupidity, fish, or yesterday evening. 
> 
> I choose instead to lie asleep at the base of a hill while shepherds work, bending the world to their tepid will. This is where I source my contempt, deep within the index of swill. Its entries omit all mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears and fell to shape the Earth—and the very base of this hill where I sunbathe, whispering “jealous cellmate” as my driven peers pass by.

***

* **Clarity & Flow:** Resolved run-on sentences and double phrasings (e.g., "with Dana Ward with Dana Ward") to establish a rhythmic, elegant cadence.
* **Elevated Diction:** Replaced casual phrases like "kind of stupid" with "peculiar/subtle foolishness" to match the poetic tone of the surrounding text without altering the meaning.
* **Preservation of Imagery:** Fully maintained every specific detail—Dana Ward, Sarah, the reader, fishing tackle reimagined as jewelry, the courtroom kitten, the shepherds, the index of swill, and the cosmic origin of the hill.

In the company of Dana Ward, I experience a complete lack of motivation. Crafting text inflicts a misery far worse than living itself; I lack any urge to write, yet I proceed out of a foolish impulse. Still, this ignorance is neither the kind Sarah attributes to me nor the version held by you, the reader, who envision me angling. 

Cord, reel, artificial bait, and hook—I view utilitarian objects merely as personal adornments. To my perception, a book of matches is simply a crown, and a fishing spinner is an elongated, pale wristlet.

A few fair-weather companions consider me a washed-up vagrant, perpetually attempting to force my confession by demanding, "Recount the events of that particular evening of heavy drinking." Put on the witness stand, I take the form of an extraordinarily precious young cat, utterly incapable of speaking about foolishness, aquatic creatures, or the previous night.

I prefer resting in slumber at the foot of an incline while herders half-heartedly attempt to control their livestock. I harvest my feelings of disdain from a catalog of refuse. That directory leaves out any listing for the underworld—a realm that was strained through a canyon of grief before falling to forge the planet, as well as the bottom of this mound where I soak up the sun. There, I softly mutter "envious inmate" whenever my driven acquaintances stride past.
outputs.L3:
A profound inertia governs my daily life. I possess no genuine desire for activity, and I find the act of writing to be an excruciating, agonizing chore. Every word feels dragged out against my will, a painful concession to a compulsion I cannot entirely explain. Yet, despite this overwhelming reluctance and my deep hatred for the effort it requires, I continue to write, bound to the very task that torments me.

This aversion to practical utility shapes my relationship with the physical world. Where others see tools of industry or recreation, I see only aesthetic trinkets. Fishing gear, rugged pocket knives, and finely crafted hardware are entirely stripped of their functional purpose in my hands. A brass reel or a woven line is not an instrument for catching fish, but a decorative accessory—an eccentric piece of jewelry to be displayed, admired, and worn, untouched by actual labor.

Draped in these useless ornaments, I prefer to lie completely idle outdoors, comfortably reclined while the rest of the world engages in disciplined effort. All around me, people throw themselves into relentless, dutiful labor, driven by a commitment to productivity that I find entirely alien. As these hardworking peers pass by my spot in the grass, their brows slick with honest sweat, I feel no admiration. Instead, I harbor a deep, quiet contempt for them, inwardly mocking their earnest struggles and taking satisfaction in my own unearned leisure.

My refusal to accept the burdens of maturity extends just as naturally to my personal relationships. On the occasions when friends corner me, demanding accountability for my past drunken escapades and reckless behavior, I offer no rationalizations or apologies. Instead, I retreat into a calculated, wide-eyed persona of complete helplessness. I remain steadfastly silent, weaponizing a look of innocent confusion until their indignation loses its edge, allowing my childish retreat to shield me from the consequences of my actions. 

In the end, I remain an unrepentant paradox: an idle observer who despises effort yet feels compelled to document it; a cynic adorned in the tools of honest work; and a silent spectator who mocks the laboring world from the safety of a cute, helpless mask.
outputs.L4:
There is a relentless, almost violent imperative in modern existence that demands continuous motion. We are instructed to strive, to build, to justify our presence on this earth through the relentless accumulation of output. Yet, looking out at this grand machinery of human effort, I am filled only with a profound, bone-deep reluctance to participate. To step into the arena of active life feels not like a noble calling, but like a surrender to an exhausting, senseless noise.

Around me, my peers move with an enviable, terrifying purpose. They measure their days in tasks accomplished and ambitions realized, casting sharp, critical glances at anyone who falters. In their eyes, my stillness is a moral failing—a shameful waste of energy, an insult to their own tireless striving. They monitor my inaction with an unspoken judgment, waiting for an apology or an awakening that will never come.

To shield myself from their demands without wasting my spirit in open conflict, I have cultivated a method of aesthetic detachment. I have learned to alter my perception of the world, stripping the objects around me of their tedious utility. To my peers, a desk is a workspace, a pen is an instrument of labor, and a coat is a functional armor against the elements. To me, they are nothing more than decorative props in a quiet, motionless tableau. I carry the briefcase not to hold papers of commerce, but because its stiff leather and cold brass hinges offer a pleasing tactile weight. I observe the clock not to measure deadlines, but to watch the hypnotic, useless arc of its bronze hands. By reinterpreting the practical instruments of daily effort as mere aesthetic accessories, I neutralize their power over me. I transform the apparatus of work into a set of harmless, meaningless ornaments.

In my interactions with the world, I maintain a stance of passive uncooperativeness. Active resistance would require an expenditure of energy I refuse to yield; it would validate the very system I despise by granting it an enemy. Instead, I offer an impenetrable, silent friction. I stand motionless within the stream of their kinetic urgency, offering neither assistance nor opposition, but simply an immovable refusal to be swept along.

My peers demand an explanation. They wish for me to name my condition—to call it sorrow, or laziness, or protest—so that they might categorize it, fix it, and drag me back into the fold of useful labor. But I grant them no such satisfaction. Explanation is a form of compliance; to justify my choices to them would be to accept the premise that I owe society an accounting of my soul. 

Ultimately, I choose the quiet dignity of withdrawal. It is a retreat born not of fear, but of a quiet, burning contempt for the altar of productivity. Let others wear themselves down in the frantic pursuit of purpose and approval. I step back into the shadows of my own choosing, leaving behind their expectations, their labor, and their judgment. In this absolute silence, stripped of the need to perform or conform, I find the only true sovereignty that remains: the freedom to simply be, untouched and unbothered by the world.
outputs.L5:
The storm beat heavily against the tall glass windows of the estate’s forgotten library, but inside, the air was thick with the scent of aged paper and ozone. 

**Ward** stood over the heavy mahogany desk, his gloved fingers carefully tracing the delicate gold leaf on a faded, hand-drawn map. He was always the cautious one, the historian who preferred certainty over impulse. "If we're wrong about these coordinates, we risk destroying a piece of history for a wild goose chase," he said, his voice measured despite the tension in the room.

**Dana** paced near the fireplace, her boots leaving damp prints on the rug. Her energy was a stark contrast to Ward’s methodical calm. She ran a hand through her hair, her eyes bright with anticipation. "We aren't wrong, Ward," she insisted, stopping to lean over the desk. "The journal entries align perfectly with the lunar cycle from 1842. We’ve double-checked every reference. Trust the research."

Before Ward could counter, the heavy oak door swung open, and **Sarah** stepped into the room. She carried a small, tarnished brass box, brushing dust from her coat. A triumphant smile played on her lips as she set the box down between Ward’s map and Dana’s scattered notes.

"You two are still arguing about the map?" Sarah asked, her voice light with amusement. "While you were analyzing the paper, I took a closer look at the hollow in the floorboards beneath the altar."

Dana grinned, stepping forward immediately. "You found it."

"I found it," Sarah confirmed, stepping back to let them both see. "It turns out we needed Ward's patience to locate the room, Dana's instinct to look beneath the floor, and a little luck."

Ward looked up from the brass box, meeting Sarah's amused gaze and Dana's eager smile. The hesitation that had held him back all evening finally vanished. With a nod, Ward reached out to lift the clasp, and together, the three of them leaned in to unlock the secret they had spent years trying to find.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the style of contemporary avant-garde poetry, dedicated to Dana Ward. Focus on themes of profound apathy, feeling judged by friends for a night of drinking, and transforming mundane objects like matchbooks and fishing lures into jewelry, transitioning into a quiet pastoral scene with subtle rhymes at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
*(for Dana Ward)*

The apathy arrives not as a void, but as a thick, milky non-feeling, an infinite plain of flat ginger ale where my own pulse sounds like a soft shoe dropped in a distant, marble museum. Across the kitchen, my friends assemble in a tight, geometric circle, their eyes ground down to silver needles, sewing my sloppy midnight speeches back into my throat. I drank until the ceiling turned into a humid, amber swamp, and now their collective stillness forms a polite, impenetrable fog; they check their phones and speak in a dialect made entirely of tiny, disappointed clocks. 

To armor my body against this soft tribunal, I kneel on the sticky linoleum and begin the work of adornment. I gather the damp bar matchbooks—*Close Cover Before Striking*—and weave them with thin wire into a jagged collar of burnt sulfur and cardboard prayer. I thread the treble hooks of Rapala fishing lures through my ears, letting the neon-green minnows and feather-dusted spinners swing like heavy, venomous gems against my collarbone. I am a glistening, absurd chandelier of tackle boxes and strike-anywheres, fully decorated for an armistice that nobody declared. 

And then, softly, the apartment unhinges itself and folds outward into open grass. The shame dissolves into a low, damp green. Out here, the wild chicory does not care how much I spilled, nor does the breeze remember my loud, unthreaded mouth. The cows stand idle in the shade, their dark eyes gentle and unmade. I walk through clover wet with dew, where nothing is old and nothing is new. A sleeping bird uncurls its wing; I lay my paper crown upon the moss, forgive the fever and the heavy loss, and listen as the quiet fields begin to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional, stream-of-consciousness monologue from the perspective of an unapologetically lazy narrator who compares themselves to a cute kitten on a witness stand.
counterfactuals.output:
Look, go ahead, read the charges, I’m not even going to sit up straight for them. *Guilty.* There, saved us all a trial, can I go back to sleep now? No, wait, look at me—no, seriously, look at me down here, squished into this corner of the sofa like a throw pillow someone forgot to fluff. You think you’re cross-examining a functioning member of the labor force, but you’re not. You’re putting a kitten on the witness stand. 

Picture it. Go on, picture a little gray tabby, three months old, sitting in that high wooden box. The prosecutor points a finger, trembling with righteous, capitalistic fury—*“Where were you on the afternoon of Tuesday the 14th when the inbox was overflowing?!”*—and what does the kitten do? It blinks. Slowly. One eye, then the other. It tilts its head, licks a single paw, and then falls over sideways because maintaining verticality is a scam invented by people who sell standing desks. 

That’s me. I am the kitten. *Your Honor, my client is simply too soft to be held accountable.* 

You can’t send a creature with pink toe-beans to prison for failing to optimize their synergy! What are you gonna do, subpoena my nap schedule? Look at my eyes, they’re huge, they’re useless, they are completely unburdened by the concept of a mortgage. I don’t *do* deadlines. I knock deadlines off the edge of the kitchen counter just to watch them fall, and then I stand there, purring, while you sweep up the glass. "Oh, did that ruin your week? That’s crazy. Anyway, my bowl is half empty, rectify this immediately or I will scream."

It’s an art form, really. Weaponized incompetence? No, no, that’s too active. This is *existential inertia*. It takes a profound, almost spiritual commitment to do absolutely nothing while the world screams around you. Society wants me to grind, to hustle, to rise and conquer the day—ew. Rise? The sun rises because it has a hydrogen-fusion reaction to deal with, I have zero fusion going on. I’m cold. I’m a cold little ball of static electricity under three layers of fleece. Movement creates friction, friction creates heat, heat causes global warming—so technically, my catatonia is an environmental service. You’re welcome, Earth. Rest easy. I know I am.

What was I supposed to be doing today? Something with a spreadsheet? A bank? A dentist? It’s all so far away. It’s on the other side of the room, and between here and there lies an ocean of hardwood floor that is slightly colder than room temperature. Impossible trek. I’d need a sled and a team of huskies. 

Besides, if you put a kitten under oath, what’s it gonna swear on? A pouch of wet food? A stray patch of sunlight moving across the rug? "Do you solemnly swear to tell the truth, the whole truth..." *Mew.* Case dismissed. Jury in tears. The bailiff is scratching me behind the ears. I win. I always win because I refuse to play. 

God, talking this much is exhausting, my mouth feels heavy. The sun just hit the armrest. Look at that yellow square right there. It’s calling to me. It’s saying, *abandon your ambitions, they never loved you anyway.* My eyelids are made of wet concrete. If the prosecution has no further questions… I’m just going to fold my hands under my chest… tuck my head into my shoulders… right here… yeah. Objection, Your Honor. The defense rests. Permanently. Don't wake me unless the house is actually on fire, and even then, make sure it’s a direct threat to this couch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic text that incorporates the following elements: Dana Ward, a reader named Sarah, fishing accessories re-imagined as fashion items, a trial or courtroom interrogation, and sleeping at the foot of a hill while shepherds work around you.
counterfactuals.output:
“State your devotion for the record,” the prosecutor said.

Sarah sat straight in the witness box,
holding a open volume of Dana Ward
like a hymnal stolen from a glittering church.
Her collar was a lattice of clear monofilament,
strung with lead sinkers that pulled her shoulders back into posture.
Her dress: an impossible evening gown of olive rubber waders,
nipped at the waist, sweeping down to the marble floor,
adorned with neon spinner-baits that clinked like chandelier glass.

From her ears swung two royal salmon flies—
emerald silk, peacock herl, and polished steel hooks 
filed down so they only teased the skin.
A red-and-white plastic bobber sat pinned to her lapel,
a high-fashion brooch floating upon her chest 
like a artificial, suspended heart.

“Did you, or did you not,” the judge leaned forward,
“let the line run out into the deep?”

Sarah turned a page of Dana Ward,
her thumb leaving a soft smudge of graphite near a stanza on tenderness.
“Objection,” she murmured to the court.
“The poetry was the lure. The water was already inside us.”

The bailiff tapped his gavel, but the sound grew muted,
muffled by the sudden smell of damp clover and sheep tallow.
The courtroom walls dissolved into misty air,
and the interrogation softened into a dream.

She was no longer on the stand,
but sleeping at the foot of a high, steep hill.
The neon lures on her dress caught the pale starlight.
Above her, invisible in the twilight, the shepherds worked.
She could hear the dry clicking of their wooden crooks,
the low, rhythmic grunts of the flock being driven across the ridge,
the whistling signals cutting through the mountain chill.

They moved around her sleep like quiet cosmos makers,
mending fences, tallying wool, ignoring the woman in haute-couture tackle
sprawled in the dew below.

And Sarah slept, her face pressed against the paper,
guilty of nothing but lingering,
while Dana’s words drifted through her hair like river grass,
and the shepherds kept the night moving around her rest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a dreamy, slightly absurd prose poem about refusing to be productive or held accountable? Address the reader directly, mention a friend named Sarah, and make it shift into rhyming verse near the end.
counterfactuals.output:
Look at you, standing there with your crisp little clipboard made of sunlight and reasonable expectations. You want to know where the quarterly report went, but I must inform you that the pages dissolved into warm butter hours ago, and I have used them to grease the wheels of my own slow-moving nap. I am simply no longer available for accountability. My ambition has taken a leave of absence to go swimming in a teacup, and I have no intention of calling it back. Yesterday, Sarah tried to hand me a list of urgent deliverables, but I gently folded her sense of dread into an origami moth and released it into the evening air. Now Sarah is lying on the rug beside me, claiming her legs have turned into melted caramel, and honestly, who am I to audit her? If you send me an email, a small starling will intercept it in mid-air, swallow your subject line, and drop a single smooth pebble into your coffee. That is my out-of-office reply. Do not ask for my billable hours; my hours have escaped into the hallway, where a very polite fox is wearing them as a scarf. 

So put down your pencil, unbuckle your shoes,
There is nothing to win, there is nothing to lose.
The spreadsheets are sleeping, the deadlines are dead,
And Sarah is crowned in a wreath of white bread.

I am floating away on a vapor of steam,
A dedicated ghost in a grand, endless dream.
No targets to hit and no forms to sign through—
I owe nothing to time, and I owe less to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary piece starting with "with Dana Ward with Dana Ward" exploring a character's deep contempt for effort and their preference for sunbathing while others work.
counterfactuals.output:
With Dana Ward with Dana Ward, the podcast on the neighbor’s deck babbles, a thin, metallic drip of voices discussing *hustle*, discussing *process*, discussing the desperate, frantic alchemy of turning sweat into moral superiority. 

I shift my hips on the canvas lounger, feeling the heat-softened vinyl adjust to the curve of my spine. I do not open my eyes. To open them would be an act of labor, an unnecessary expenditure of optical kinetic energy. Instead, I prefer the sun filtered through the pink, translucent film of my eyelids—a private, blood-warm cathedral dedicated to absolute stillness.

Across the cedar fence, Arthur is doing something unforgivable with a spade. 

I can map his movements entirely by sound: the wet *crunch* of steel severing earth, the sharp heave of his lungs, the soggy, rhythmic slap of his damp cotton shirt against his ribs. He is planting hydrangeas, or perhaps digging a trench, or constructing some other pathetic monument to human anxiety. It is a grotesque spectacle, really, this relentless, violent urge to edit the world. 

Why dig? Why bend? Why exhaust the marrow of your bone for a square yard of dirt? There is a deep, almost religious vulgarity to effort. Effort is an admission of lack. It is a loud, sweaty confession that you are currently insufficient, that your surroundings are insufficient, and that the universe made a mistake that only your twitching, strained muscles can correct. 

How intensely embarrassing. 

I reach down—slowly, moving with the glacial grace of an apex predator that has long since outgrown the need to hunt—and trace a line of oil across my collarbone. Coconut and zinc. The scent of absolute, unbothered luxury. The sun today is a golden anvil, tenderly hammering me flat, pressing me into the warmth of the afternoon until the boundary between my skin and the air dissolves completely. I am becoming photosynthetically arrogant. I do not bloom; I simply absorb.

Arthur grunts. A shovel-full of gravel rattles into a metal wheelbarrow with a harsh, brassy roar. 

Poor, twitching creature. He believes in the god of the kinetic. He has swallowed the terrible lie that the idle hand is a workshop for sin, when in reality, the idle body is the only thing on this planet that isn't actively destroying it. Look at him: his neck is the color of a slapped cheek, his lumbar spine will betray him by dusk, and for what? A row of blue blossoms that will brown at the edges before the equinox? 

To strive is to panic. To sweat is to faint in the face of existence.

I alter my breathing, dropping it into the lowest gear possible. The lizard baking on the brick wall understands this. The dry rot in the deck timber understands this. We are the true aristocrats of the afternoon. We know that the highest form of wisdom is total surrender to gravity. Let the fools build their pyramids and weed their gravel paths; the sun shines on the idle and the industrious alike, but only the idle have the sense to enjoy the burn.

On the radio, the voice repeats the credit—*interview conducted with Dana Ward with Dana Ward*—before fading into a symphony of ambient noise. I let out a breath so faint it barely disturbs the hot air above my lips. 

Let them speak of work. Let them bleed for their tiny, temporary achievements. I close my mouth, sink an inch deeper into the canvas, and let the afternoon cook me alive, perfectly, gloriously useless.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
